q: Testosterone in the human male is secreted by the:
o: Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules
x: The interstitial (Leydig) cells lying between the seminiferous tubules secrete testosterone. Sertoli cells nourish developing sperm; they do not make testosterone.

q: Sperm are produced in the:
x: Spermatogenesis takes place in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. The epididymis stores and matures sperm, and the vas deferens carries them onwards.

q: The main function of Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules is to:
o: Nourish and support the developing sperm cells
x: Sertoli cells support and nourish the cells undergoing spermatogenesis. Testosterone comes from the interstitial cells, and fructose-rich fluid from the seminal vesicles.

q: In the human male, luteinising hormone (LH) acts on the:
x: In males LH stimulates the interstitial (Leydig) cells to secrete testosterone; for this reason it is also called interstitial cell-stimulating hormone (ICSH).

q: In the human male, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) mainly:
o: Stimulates the interstitial cells to secrete testosterone
Stimulates spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules
Causes contraction of the vas deferens
Stimulates the prostate to secrete its fluid
x: FSH acts on the seminiferous tubules (through the Sertoli cells) to promote sperm production. Stimulating testosterone secretion by interstitial cells is the role of LH.

q: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is secreted by the:
x: GnRH is a hypothalamic hormone. It travels to the anterior pituitary and stimulates it to release FSH and LH, which then act on the gonads.

q: The correct order of the path taken by sperm from their site of formation to the outside is:
o: Seminiferous tubules → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra
Seminiferous tubules → vas deferens → epididymis → urethra
Epididymis → seminiferous tubules → vas deferens → urethra
Seminiferous tubules → epididymis → urethra → vas deferens
x: Sperm form in the seminiferous tubules, pass into the epididymis where they mature and are stored, then travel through the vas deferens and ejaculatory duct into the urethra.

q: Sperm leaving the testis complete their maturation and are stored in the:
x: The epididymis, a long coiled tube on the testis, stores sperm and is where they mature and gain the ability to swim. The seminal vesicle and prostate add fluids but do not store sperm.

q: The fructose-rich fluid that provides energy to sperm is secreted by the:
x: The seminal vesicles secrete a thick fluid rich in fructose, which sperm use as a source of energy. Cowper's glands secrete a lubricating mucus.

q: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands of the male secrete:
o: A clear mucus that lubricates the urethra
x: Cowper's glands release a small amount of clear mucus into the urethra that lubricates it. Fructose comes from the seminal vesicles and testosterone from the interstitial cells.

q: The testes lie outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum because:
o: Testosterone can only be made at a temperature above body temperature
The scrotum secretes the fructose needed by sperm
Spermatogenesis requires a temperature slightly lower than body temperature
Sperm need direct contact with air to become motile
x: Sperm production needs a temperature a little below normal body temperature, which the scrotum provides. The scrotum does not secrete fluids for sperm.

q: The vas deferens joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the:
x: On each side the vas deferens unites with the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the urethra within the prostate.

q: During spermatogenesis, the first cells to be haploid are the:
x: Diploid primary spermatocytes complete meiosis I to give haploid secondary spermatocytes. Spermatids are also haploid, but they arise later from meiosis II, so they are not the first.

q: One primary spermatocyte, after completing meiosis, finally gives rise to:
o: One sperm and three polar bodies
x: Meiosis I gives two secondary spermatocytes and meiosis II gives four spermatids, all of which develop into sperm. Polar bodies are formed only in oogenesis.

q: One primary oocyte that completes meiosis gives rise to:
o: One functional ovum and polar bodies
Two ova and two polar bodies
One ovum and no polar bodies
x: In oogenesis the cytoplasm divides unequally, so one large ovum is formed and the small cells left over are polar bodies, which degenerate.

q: At ovulation in a human female, the cell released from the ovary is a:
o: Mature ovum that has completed meiosis II
Secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II
Primary oocyte arrested in prophase I
Oogonium that has not begun meiosis
x: The primary oocyte completes meiosis I just before ovulation, so a secondary oocyte is released. It stays arrested in metaphase II and completes meiosis II only if a sperm enters it.

q: The second meiotic division of the human secondary oocyte is completed:
o: When a sperm enters the oocyte
When the follicle begins to grow
x: Meiosis II in the secondary oocyte is completed only after a sperm penetrates it at fertilisation, producing the ovum and a second polar body.

q: Primary oocytes form in the ovary before birth and remain arrested until puberty or later. They are arrested at:
x: Primary oocytes enter meiosis before birth and stop in prophase I. Meiosis I resumes only in the follicle that is about to ovulate; the metaphase II arrest belongs to the secondary oocyte.

q: The change of spermatids into motile sperm, without any further cell division, is called:
x: Spermiogenesis is the differentiation of spermatids into sperm: they form a head, acrosome and tail. No division takes place, unlike meiosis II, which produces the spermatids.

q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the:
x: Sperm meet the secondary oocyte in the oviduct, usually in its upper part. The fertilised egg then moves to the uterus for implantation.

q: The early embryo implants in the wall of the:
x: The embryo implants in the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus, where the placenta later develops.

q: The finger-like fimbriae at the open end of the oviduct help to:
o: Sweep the released oocyte into the oviduct
x: The funnel-shaped open end of the oviduct, fringed with fimbriae, lies close to the ovary and draws the released oocyte into the tube. Oocytes are produced in the ovary, not the oviduct.

q: The narrow lower neck of the uterus that opens into the vagina is the:
x: The cervix is the narrow neck of the uterus that projects into the vagina. The infundibulum and fimbriae belong to the ovary end of the oviduct.

q: Which change at puberty in boys is caused by testosterone?
o: Deepening of the voice and growth of facial hair
x: Testosterone produces male secondary sexual characteristics such as a deeper voice, facial and body hair and increased muscle mass. Breast development is due to oestrogen.

q: Development of the breasts and widening of the hips in girls at puberty is mainly due to:
x: Oestrogen from the ovarian follicles produces female secondary sexual characteristics. Progesterone mainly prepares the uterus for pregnancy.

q: A rise in the blood testosterone level of a man leads to:
o: Reduced secretion of GnRH and LH
Increased secretion of GnRH and LH
Increased secretion of FSH by the hypothalamus
x: Testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, reducing GnRH and LH secretion. This keeps the testosterone level steady. FSH comes from the pituitary, not the hypothalamus.

q: If the interstitial cells of a man's testes were destroyed, which change in his blood would be expected?
o: Testosterone stays the same and LH falls
x: Without interstitial cells, testosterone falls. The negative feedback that testosterone normally exerts on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost, so LH secretion rises.

q: The correct order in the hormonal control of the testes is:
x: The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which makes the anterior pituitary secrete FSH and LH. These act on the testes, which produce sperm and testosterone.

q: Which of the following structures belongs to the female reproductive system?
x: The oviduct (Fallopian tube) carries the oocyte from the ovary to the uterus. The epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicle are all male structures.

q: The male gland that surrounds the urethra just below the urinary bladder is the:
x: The prostate gland surrounds the first part of the urethra below the bladder and adds its secretion to semen. The seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder, and Cowper's glands lie lower down.

q: In the human male, which duct carries both urine and semen?
x: The male urethra is shared by the urinary and reproductive systems, carrying urine and, at other times, semen. The ureter carries only urine from kidney to bladder; the vas deferens and ejaculatory duct carry only sperm and fluid.

q: Which statement correctly compares spermatogenesis and oogenesis in humans?
o: Spermatogenesis continues through adult life, while oogenesis begins before birth
Both produce four functional gametes from each primary cell
Spermatogenesis begins before birth and stops at puberty
Oogenesis is completed inside the ovary before ovulation
x: Sperm are made continuously from puberty onwards, whereas oogenesis starts before birth with primary oocytes. Oogenesis gives one ovum per primary oocyte and is completed only after fertilisation, in the oviduct.

q: The average length of the human menstrual cycle is about:
x: The menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days on average, though it varies between women. Ovulation occurs near the middle of the cycle.

q: Menstruation is the shedding of the:
x: During menstruation the thickened endometrium breaks down and is discharged with blood through the vagina. The corpus luteum degenerates in the ovary but is not shed.

q: Ovulation is directly triggered by:
o: A rise in progesterone from the corpus luteum
A fall in oestrogen to its lowest level
x: A sudden mid-cycle surge of LH from the anterior pituitary causes the mature follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte. Progesterone rises only after ovulation.

q: During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, the main source of oestrogen is the:
x: Cells of the developing follicle secrete oestrogen, and the amount rises as the follicle grows. The corpus luteum forms only after ovulation, and the pituitary secretes FSH and LH, not oestrogen.

q: In a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, ovulation occurs at about:
x: Ovulation takes place around the middle of the cycle, about day 14 of a 28-day cycle. Day 1 is the first day of menstrual bleeding.

q: The main hormone secreted by the corpus luteum is:
x: The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone, along with some oestrogen. FSH and LH come from the anterior pituitary and GnRH from the hypothalamus.

q: The corpus luteum develops from:
o: The anterior pituitary under the effect of LH
The remains of the follicle after ovulation
x: After ovulation, LH converts the cells of the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum, a temporary endocrine structure in the ovary.

q: If the released oocyte is not fertilised, the corpus luteum:
o: Grows larger and secretes more progesterone
Changes into a new Graafian follicle
Degenerates, so the progesterone level falls
x: Without pregnancy the corpus luteum degenerates after about two weeks. Progesterone and oestrogen levels fall, and the endometrium breaks down as menstruation.

q: Menstrual bleeding begins because of:
o: A fall in progesterone and oestrogen levels
A surge of LH from the anterior pituitary
A rise in oestrogen from a new follicle
A rise in FSH acting on the uterus
x: When the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone and oestrogen fall. The endometrium can no longer be maintained, so it breaks down and is shed.

q: In the female, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) mainly:
o: Causes the rupture of the mature follicle
Stimulates the growth of ovarian follicles
x: FSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates follicles in the ovary to grow and secrete oestrogen. Rupture of the follicle at ovulation is caused by the LH surge.

q: After menstruation, the endometrium is repaired and rebuilt mainly under the influence of:
x: In the proliferative (follicular) phase, rising oestrogen from the growing follicle causes the endometrium to repair and thicken. Progesterone acts later, after ovulation.

q: Progesterone prepares the uterus for pregnancy by:
o: Causing the endometrium to be shed
Making the endometrium thick, glandular and rich in blood vessels
Stimulating new follicles to grow in the ovary
Causing contractions that expel the embryo
x: Progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the endometrium thick, glandular and well supplied with blood, ready to receive an embryo. Shedding happens when progesterone falls.

q: The phase of the menstrual cycle that follows ovulation is the:
x: After ovulation the corpus luteum forms, so this phase is called the luteal phase; in the uterus it is the secretory phase. The follicular (proliferative) phase comes before ovulation.

q: Blood progesterone concentration is highest during the:
o: Hours just before the LH surge
x: Progesterone is secreted mainly by the corpus luteum, so it peaks in the luteal phase. It is low during menstruation and the follicular phase, before any corpus luteum exists.

q: No new follicle normally matures during the luteal phase because:
o: The ovary has no follicles left after ovulation
High progesterone and oestrogen inhibit FSH and LH secretion
The LH surge destroys all remaining follicles
The endometrium secretes a hormone that blocks the ovary
x: Progesterone and oestrogen from the corpus luteum exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, keeping FSH and LH low. Without FSH, new follicles do not mature.

q: If fertilisation and implantation occur, the corpus luteum:
o: Persists and continues to secrete progesterone
Begins to secrete FSH and LH
x: In pregnancy the corpus luteum is maintained and keeps secreting progesterone, so the endometrium is not shed and menstruation stops. Later the placenta takes over this role.

q: A mature ovarian follicle that is ready to release its oocyte is called a:
x: The fully mature, fluid-filled follicle is the Graafian follicle; it ruptures at ovulation. The corpus luteum forms from it afterwards, and the corpus albicans is the scar left when the corpus luteum degenerates.

q: The first few days of the menstrual cycle, when bleeding occurs, form the:
x: The cycle is counted from the first day of bleeding, so the menstrual phase comes first, lasting about 3–5 days. The luteal (secretory) phase comes after ovulation.

q: FSH and LH, which control the ovarian cycle, are secreted by the:
x: Both gonadotrophins, FSH and LH, are made by the anterior pituitary under the control of GnRH from the hypothalamus. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH.

q: A woman's blood test shows high progesterone, moderately high oestrogen, and low FSH and LH. These levels match which part of her menstrual cycle?
o: The time of the LH surge
x: High progesterone means an active corpus luteum, which exists only in the luteal phase; its hormones also hold FSH and LH low by negative feedback. During menstruation and the early follicular phase progesterone is low, and at the surge LH is high.

q: Which is the correct order of ovarian events in a cycle without pregnancy?
o: Corpus luteum forms → follicle grows → ovulation → corpus luteum degenerates
Ovulation → follicle grows → corpus luteum forms → corpus luteum degenerates
Follicle grows → ovulation → corpus luteum forms → corpus luteum degenerates
Follicle grows → corpus luteum forms → ovulation → corpus luteum degenerates
x: A follicle matures under FSH, ruptures at ovulation under the LH surge, and its remains form the corpus luteum, which degenerates if no pregnancy occurs.

q: Which statement about the feedback effects of oestrogen in the menstrual cycle is correct?
o: Moderate levels inhibit FSH, but a high level before mid-cycle triggers the LH surge
Oestrogen always stimulates FSH and LH at every level
Oestrogen has no effect on the pituitary; only progesterone does
A high level of oestrogen before mid-cycle suppresses LH and so prevents ovulation
x: Moderate oestrogen in the early follicular phase exerts negative feedback on FSH. When oestrogen from the mature follicle becomes high, it has a positive feedback effect that produces the LH surge and ovulation.

q: When the corpus luteum degenerates at the end of a cycle, FSH secretion:
o: Increases, because inhibition by progesterone and oestrogen is removed
Is unaffected, because FSH is controlled only by LH
x: Falling progesterone and oestrogen remove the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so FSH rises and a new follicle begins to develop for the next cycle.

q: The release of a secondary oocyte from the ovary is called:
x: Ovulation is the release of the secondary oocyte from a ruptured Graafian follicle. Implantation is the embedding of the embryo in the uterus.

q: If pregnancy does not occur, the corpus luteum remains active for about:
o: The rest of the woman's reproductive life
x: Without pregnancy the corpus luteum functions for roughly the length of the luteal phase, about two weeks, and then degenerates, after which menstruation begins.

q: A drug keeps a woman's blood progesterone and oestrogen continuously high. What is the expected effect on her ovaries?
o: An LH surge occurs every week
Ovulation is prevented because FSH and LH are suppressed
The corpus luteum forms without ovulation
x: Constantly high progesterone and oestrogen exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary. FSH and LH stay low, so follicles do not mature and no LH surge occurs.

q: The endometrium is at its thickest and most glandular during the:
x: The endometrium thickens under oestrogen and then becomes most developed under progesterone in the late luteal phase, ready for implantation. It is thinnest during and just after menstruation.

q: The menstrual cycle is regulated by hormones from the:
x: GnRH from the hypothalamus controls FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary, which act on the ovaries. Oestrogen and progesterone from the ovaries then control the uterus and feed back on the brain.

q: In the female reproductive cycle, GnRH from the hypothalamus acts directly on the:
o: Uterus, causing thickening of the endometrium
Anterior pituitary, causing release of FSH and LH
x: GnRH travels to the anterior pituitary and stimulates release of FSH and LH. It does not act directly on the ovary or uterus; those are controlled by the pituitary and ovarian hormones.

q: The follicular phase of the ovary takes place at the same time as which phase of the uterus?
x: While the follicle grows and secretes oestrogen (follicular phase), the endometrium rebuilds and thickens (proliferative phase). The secretory phase matches the ovary's luteal phase.

q: The corpus luteum is found in the:
x: The corpus luteum forms in the ovary from the ruptured follicle after ovulation and secretes progesterone.

q: A woman with a regular 28-day cycle starts menstrual bleeding on 1 March. Ovulation is expected around:
x: Day 1 of the cycle is the first day of bleeding (1 March). Ovulation occurs about day 14 of a 28-day cycle, so around 14 March.

q: Gonorrhoea is caused by:
x: Gonorrhoea is a bacterial infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Treponema pallidum causes syphilis.

q: The causative agent of syphilis is:
x: Syphilis is caused by the spiral bacterium Treponema pallidum. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhoea.

q: In untreated syphilis, the long stage without symptoms that can last for years between the secondary and tertiary stages is called the:
x: After the secondary rash fades, syphilis enters a latent stage with no symptoms, although the bacteria remain in the body. The incubation period comes before the primary chancre, not after the secondary stage.

q: Genital herpes is caused by:
x: Genital herpes is a viral infection caused by herpes simplex virus. HIV causes AIDS, and the two bacteria cause syphilis and gonorrhoea.

q: Treponema pallidum, the cause of syphilis, is a:
x: Treponema pallidum is a thin, spiral bacterium called a spirochaete. The Gram-negative diplococcus is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the cause of gonorrhoea.

q: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is best described as a:
x: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative coccus that occurs in pairs (a diplococcus). Spirochaetes include Treponema pallidum, and HIV is an enveloped RNA virus.

q: Which of the following diseases is NOT caused by a virus?
x: Syphilis is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. Genital herpes (herpes simplex virus), AIDS (HIV) and polio (poliovirus) are all viral diseases.

q: Syphilis can pass from an infected pregnant mother to her fetus because Treponema pallidum can:
o: Remain latent in the mother's nerve cells
x: Treponema pallidum can cross the placenta and infect the fetus, causing congenital syphilis. Latency in nerve cells is a feature of herpes simplex virus, not syphilis.

q: Which statement about genital herpes is correct?
o: The virus can be passed on even when no sores are visible
A short course of antibiotics removes the virus completely
It is caused by a spiral-shaped bacterium
One attack gives lifelong immunity, so sores never return
x: Herpes simplex virus can be passed on between outbreaks, even when no sores are seen. It is a virus, so antibiotics do not cure it, and it stays latent in nerve cells, so sores often return.

q: Gonorrhoea is spread mainly by:
o: Sexual contact with an infected person
x: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease; Neisseria gonorrhoeae passes between partners during sexual contact. It is not spread by water, insects or air.

q: A main symptom of gonorrhoea in men is:
o: A single painless ulcer on the penis
Painful fluid-filled blisters that come and go
Painful urination with a pus-like discharge from the urethra
Long-lasting fever with severe weight loss
x: Gonorrhoea inflames the urethra, causing burning or painful urination and a pus-like discharge. A painless ulcer suggests syphilis, and recurring blisters suggest genital herpes.

q: The characteristic symptom of genital herpes is:
o: A painless hard ulcer called a chancre
Painful blisters or sores on the genitals
A skin rash on the palms and soles
Thick pus discharge from the urethra
x: Herpes simplex virus causes painful fluid-filled blisters that break into sores on and around the genitals. A painless chancre and a palm-and-sole rash are features of syphilis.

q: Genital herpes often returns in repeated episodes even after the sores heal. This is because the virus:
o: Is quickly destroyed and the person is reinfected each time
Multiplies only in red blood cells
Remains latent in nerve cells and becomes active again later
x: After the first attack, herpes simplex virus stays dormant in nerve cells. It can reactivate later and travel back to the skin, producing new sores. Antibiotics do not act on viruses at all.

q: The chancre of primary syphilis usually heals by itself within a few weeks, even without treatment. This means that:
o: The person is cured and can no longer spread the infection
The infection must have been caused by a virus
The bacteria may remain and the disease can progress to later stages
Treatment will not be needed at any later stage
x: Healing of the chancre is not a cure: Treponema pallidum spreads through the body and, if untreated, causes secondary and, years later, tertiary syphilis.

q: Both syphilis and genital herpes can cause sores on the genitals. A key difference is that:
o: Syphilis causes painful blisters, while the herpes sore is a painless ulcer
The syphilis chancre is usually painless, while herpes causes painful blisters
Herpes sores contain spiral bacteria, while syphilis sores contain a virus
Syphilis sores keep returning from a virus in nerves, while herpes sores appear once
x: Primary syphilis gives a single painless ulcer (chancre) caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. Genital herpes, caused by herpes simplex virus, gives painful fluid-filled blisters that often return.

q: Years after an untreated infection, the tertiary stage of syphilis can cause:
o: Damage to the nervous system, heart and blood vessels
A single painless chancre at the site of entry
Painful genital blisters that keep recurring
x: In tertiary syphilis the bacteria damage internal organs such as the brain, spinal cord, heart and blood vessels. The chancre belongs to the primary stage.

q: A skin rash (often on the palms and soles), fever and swollen lymph nodes are typical of which stage of syphilis?
x: The secondary stage follows the chancre and shows a widespread skin rash, fever and swollen lymph nodes. The latent stage has no symptoms, and the tertiary stage damages internal organs.

q: Which statement about gonorrhoea in women is correct?
o: It always produces a painless chancre
It is caused by a spirochaete bacterium
It may cause few or no symptoms, yet can damage the oviducts and cause infertility
It is caused by a virus that hides in nerve cells
x: In many women gonorrhoea is mild or symptomless, so it may go unnoticed while spreading to the oviducts, where it can cause scarring and infertility. Its cause is a diplococcus bacterium, not a spirochaete or a virus.

q: A baby born to a mother with untreated gonorrhoea is at particular risk of infection of the:
x: Neisseria gonorrhoeae can infect a newborn's eyes during passage through the birth canal, causing a serious eye infection that can lead to blindness.

q: Which of the following is NOT a usual feature of gonorrhoea?
o: A pus-like discharge from the urethra
Few or no symptoms in many infected women
A single painless hard ulcer at the site of infection
x: Gonorrhoea typically causes painful urination and a pus-like discharge, and it is often silent in women. A single painless hard ulcer (chancre) is the sign of primary syphilis.

q: HIV can pass from an infected mother to her child through:
o: Only by touching the baby's skin
The placenta, during birth, or in breast milk
Sharing the same room with the baby
x: Mother-to-child transmission of HIV can occur across the placenta, during delivery, or through breastfeeding. It is not spread by insects or ordinary touch.

q: People with AIDS suffer infections by organisms that rarely harm healthy people. The main reason is that:
o: The loss of helper T cells weakens both antibody and cell-mediated immunity
HIV destroys red blood cells, so tissues lack oxygen
HIV directly makes harmless microbes more virulent
Antibiotics stop working in people infected with HIV
x: Helper T cells are needed to activate B cells (antibodies) and cytotoxic T cells. When HIV destroys them, the whole immune response fails, so opportunistic infections take hold.

q: Three weeks after sexual exposure, a man develops a single painless genital ulcer. Fluid from it shows spiral bacteria. The disease and its agent are:
x: A painless ulcer (chancre) with spiral bacteria is primary syphilis, caused by the spirochaete Treponema pallidum. Neisseria is a diplococcus, and herpes gives painful blisters.

q: Which comparison of gonorrhoea and syphilis is correct?
o: Gonorrhoea is viral, while syphilis is bacterial
Both begin with a painless chancre as the first sign
Both are bacterial, but only syphilis progresses through stages that can affect organs years later
Syphilis is caused by a diplococcus and gonorrhoea by a spirochaete
x: Both diseases are caused by bacteria: gonorrhoea by a diplococcus and syphilis by a spirochaete. Syphilis passes through primary, secondary and tertiary stages, while the chancre is a sign of syphilis only.

q: Which pair of STDs can be treated with antibiotics?
x: Antibiotics act on bacteria, so they can treat gonorrhoea and syphilis. Genital herpes and AIDS are viral diseases, which antibiotics cannot cure.

q: Which statement about HIV infection is correct?
o: An infected person may have no symptoms for years but can still pass on the virus
Symptoms always appear within a day of infection
The virus is killed by a short course of penicillin
The virus is spread by mosquito bites
x: HIV has a long period, often years, during which the person may feel well but can still transmit the virus. Antibiotics such as penicillin do not act on viruses.

q: The herpes simplex virus that causes genital herpes is a:
x: Herpes simplex virus is an enveloped DNA virus. HIV is the RNA retrovirus among the STD agents, and the two bacteria cause syphilis and gonorrhoea.

q: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the cause of gonorrhoea, mainly infects the:
o: Helper T lymphocytes in the blood
Mucous membranes lining the urethra and cervix
Nerve cells near the spinal cord
Skin of the palms and soles
x: Gonococci infect the moist mucous membranes of the urinary and reproductive tracts, such as the urethra and cervix, causing discharge and painful urination. Helper T cells are the target of HIV, and herpes virus hides in nerve cells.

q: The term 'chancre' refers to the:
x: A chancre is the painless, firm ulcer that appears where Treponema pallidum entered the body, the sign of primary syphilis. It usually heals on its own even though the infection continues.

q: Which of the following is a cancer commonly seen in people with AIDS?
x: Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer of blood-vessel tissue, is common when immunity is destroyed by HIV. Hemophilia and sickle-cell anaemia are inherited disorders, and diabetes is a metabolic disease.

q: In a person with untreated HIV infection, which blood finding becomes more marked as the infection progresses to AIDS?
o: A rising number of helper T cells
A rising red blood cell count
A steadily falling number of virus particles
A falling number of helper T cells
x: HIV steadily destroys helper T (CD4) cells, so their number falls as the disease advances, while the amount of virus usually rises. AIDS develops when helper T cells become very low.
